topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the local sign object participates in a broader Quranic verdict pattern.
topics.reason: The rows tie the sign root to denial, punishment, same-surah recurrence, and cross-surah verdict contexts.

words.gloss_range: proper divine name in genitive construct, marking the signs as God's
words.prose: {{ar:ٱللَّهِ}} ({{tr:Allāhi}}) fixes the signs as God's signs by construct, not as generic evidence or direct bare denial of God. The name then becomes the antecedent for the suffix in {{ar:لِقَآئِهِۦٓ}} ({{tr:liqāʾihī}}), before the discourse turns even more direct in {{ar:رَّحْمَتِى}} ({{tr:raḥmatī}}). That reference chain keeps signs, meeting, mercy, and punishment under one divine accountability frame.

topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the divine reference moving from named source to pronoun to first-person mercy without changing referent.
topics.reason: The divine name is the genitive complement of the sign construct and supplies the antecedent for the later meeting suffix.

topics.headline: proper name blocks generic deity reading
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the signs and meeting belong to the singular divine referent, while broader worship/bewilderment pressures remain secondary.
topics.reason: QAC marks the word as a proper noun; lexical disputes can color the divine field but do not override the proper-name function.

words.gloss_range: coordinating conjunction that adds the meeting as a second denied object
words.prose: The second {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) binds {{ar:لِقَآئِهِۦٓ}} ({{tr:liqāʾihī}}) to {{ar:ـَٔايَٰتِ}} ({{tr:āyāti}}) under the already active {{ar:بِ}} ({{tr:bi}}). It is therefore not a loose addition; it makes denial of present signs travel with denial of the future meeting, creating a temporal escalation inside one object chain.

words.gloss_range: construct gerund for His meeting, the eschatological encounter coordinated under denial
words.prose: {{ar:لِقَآئِهِۦٓ}} ({{tr:liqāʾihī}}) is not introduced by a fresh preposition; its initial lām is part of the root, while the whole gerund remains a second object coordinated under {{ar:بِ}} ({{tr:bi}}). The suffix makes the meeting specifically His, and the maṣdar form treats that encounter as a settled reality capable of being denied. Its local force is accountable divine meeting, with broader encounter/confrontation and casting-family pressures kept as color, and 29:5 supplies a sharp same-surah contrast between hoping for the meeting and denying it. The long vowel and hamza also slow this second object before the demonstrative verdict reset.

words.gloss_range: far demonstrative resuming the denier class before the first verdict
words.prose: The first {{ar:أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ}} ({{tr:ulāʾika}}) resumes the long relative subject and points at it from evaluative distance before the first verdict. As a demonstrative subject with a verbal predicate, it turns the charge into a formal pronouncement: those ones have despaired. Its shape also begins the repeated demonstrative frame that will split despair and punishment into two panels.

topics.headline: demonstrative gathers the long subject
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the predicate is attached to a deliberately recalled class, not to a vague preceding phrase.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence marks this demonstrative as appositional resumption and subject of the despair verb.

topics.headline: far deixis distances the deniers
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the grammar points to the deniers as morally distant before naming despair.
topics.reason: The form is the far demonstrative and is used after the denier class has been defined.

topics.headline: first pointer sets up the repeated verdict frame
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the architecture of paired verdicts beginning before the first predicate arrives.
topics.reason: The same demonstrative recurs in the second verdict clause, creating a matched frame.

words.gloss_range: perfect plural verb of despair completed by {{ar:مِنْ}} ({{tr:min}})
words.prose: {{ar:يَئِسُوا۟}} ({{tr:yaʾisū}}) is perfect even though it begins with yāʾ; the yāʾ is a root consonant, and the plural suffix keeps the same deniers in view. Its complement must come through {{ar:مِنْ}} ({{tr:min}}), so mercy is framed as the domain from which hope is cut off. The rare despair root is locally selected over the dialectal knowledge sense, but that note sharpens the verdict as recognized exclusion; echoes such as 12:87 and the 29:5 hope contrast make denial and despair mutually illuminating.
words.root_gloss_range: despair, loss of hope, and in some dialectal evidence recognized knowledge; local complement selects despair from mercy

topics.headline: despair answers denial and reverses hope
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the first verdict stands on a Quranic axis where deniers despair of divine relief (12:87) and where hope for the meeting appears earlier in this surah (29:5).
topics.reason: The rows give 12:87 and 29:5 as concrete anchors, and the local ayah places denial before despair from mercy.

words.gloss_range: preposition marking separation from and specification of the mercy-domain
words.prose: {{ar:مِنْ}} ({{tr:min}}) completes {{ar:يَئِسُوا۟}} ({{tr:yaʾisū}}) by marking the mercy-domain from which hope is lost. Its strongest local force is separation/source, with a partitive pressure that makes the loss sharper: not even a share from {{ar:رَّحْمَتِى}} ({{tr:raḥmatī}}) remains accessible in the verdict. The phrase also closes the first panel before the next {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) opens punishment.

topics.headline: even a portion of mercy is out of reach

words.gloss_range: My mercy: a genitive verbal noun with first-person divine possessive suffix
words.prose: {{ar:رَّحْمَتِى}} ({{tr:raḥmatī}}) is where the ayah's divine reference becomes direct: after {{ar:ٱللَّهِ}} ({{tr:Allāhi}}) and His meeting, the suffix says My mercy. The noun can name mercy as a domain, state, or divine act, and the womb-care root image makes despair feel like exclusion from encompassing nurture. This mercy is then balanced against {{ar:عَذَابٌ}} ({{tr:ʿadhābun}}): what is lost is personally claimed mercy, what is assigned is punishment, and the anti-despair mercy call of 39:53 sharpens the contrast.
words.root_gloss_range: mercy, compassion, grace, care, and womb-like nurture; local suffix makes it God's own mercy or merciful action

topics.headline: lost mercy balances assigned punishment

topics.reason: The rows connect mercy with despair and punishment, cite 39:53, and link the boundary movement from lost support to lost divine mercy.

words.gloss_range: conjunction joining the despair verdict to the punishment verdict
words.prose: The {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) before the second {{ar:أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ}} ({{tr:ulāʾika}}) joins the despair panel to a second verdict panel. Because it is {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}), not a result particle, the punishment is coordinated as a cumulative sentence rather than merely narrated as the next event. Its short reset makes the repeated demonstrative arrive as a formal second pronouncement.

topics.headline: sequence pressure without fa-causality
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that punishment follows despair in order and force, but the grammar does not reduce it to a mechanical result event.
topics.reason: The local connector is {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}), so cumulative sequencing is valid while strict result-particle force is not.

words.gloss_range: repeated far demonstrative reopening the same subject for the punishment clause
words.prose: The repeated {{ar:أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ}} ({{tr:ulāʾika}}) re-identifies the same deniers at distance before the punishment clause. It is not a new group; it is a solemn re-pointing that changes predicate type, from the verbal {{ar:يَئِسُوا۟}} ({{tr:yaʾisū}}) to the nominal possession frame {{ar:لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ}} ({{tr:lahum ʿadhābun}}). That repetition is what makes the ayah's sentencing two-stage rather than a single compressed predicate.

words.prose: {{ar:لَ}} ({{tr:la}}) in {{ar:لَهُمْ}} ({{tr:lahum}}) assigns the punishment before the noun is even named. The fronted prepositional predicate foregrounds the recipients, so the clause first says for them, then reveals {{ar:عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ}} ({{tr:ʿadhābun alīmun}}). The lām's possession, specification, and settled-assignment values converge into an ironic possession: what is theirs is punishment.

words.gloss_range: third-person plural pronoun compressing the denier class as punishment recipients
words.prose: {{ar:هُمْ}} ({{tr:hum}}) is the compressed final link in the referent chain: {{ar:ٱلَّذِينَ}} ({{tr:alladhīna}}), then two instances of {{ar:أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ}} ({{tr:ulāʾika}}), then this pronoun inside {{ar:لَهُمْ}} ({{tr:lahum}}). It does not introduce new agents; governed by the lām, it makes the already-defined deniers the recipients of punishment. The ayah thus moves from described class to pointed group to compact assigned recipient.

words.gloss_range: indefinite nominative punishment noun, delayed after the recipient phrase
words.prose: {{ar:عَذَابٌ}} ({{tr:ʿadhābun}}) arrives after {{ar:لَهُمْ}} ({{tr:lahum}}) as an indefinite nominative subject: punishment is what has been established for them. Its indefiniteness keeps the punishment open-ended and magnified, while concord binds the following {{ar:أَلِيمٌۭ}} ({{tr:alīmun}}) to it as modifier. The root's withholding and sweet-water contrast sharpen the move from lost {{ar:رَّحْمَتِى}} ({{tr:raḥmatī}}) to assigned deprivation, and the phrase also joins a dominant punishment-pain formula carried elsewhere in the surah such as 29:53.

words.gloss_range: indefinite nominative adjective qualifying punishment as painful
words.prose: {{ar:أَلِيمٌۭ}} ({{tr:alīmun}}) is the final adjective, agreeing with {{ar:عَذَابٌ}} ({{tr:ʿadhābun}}) in case and indefiniteness and sealing the phrase as painful punishment rather than a separate predicate. Its faʿīl shape can compress pain-causing and painfully-felt force, so the last word turns abstract punishment into felt experience. Formulaic recurrence matters, but here the formula lands after this ayah's distinctive chain: signs denied, meeting denied, mercy despaired of, punishment assigned, pain named. The near-homophonous pressure beside ʿalīm remains only a controlled sound tension; the local root and final sense stay with pain.
